claims.text: Tailored thermo-mechanical processing can induce grain-boundary and phase-interface segregation of Cr or Al while keeping the overall alloy composition constant.
Cr and Al promote the formation of protective Cr2O3 and Al2O3 scales, respectively.
Segregation of oxophilic elements at grain boundaries and phase interfaces facilitates nucleation and growth of a dense, continuous protective oxide at those sites.
A dense and continuous protective scale suppresses inward oxygen diffusion and outward metal-cation transport.
Suppressing oxygen and metal-cation transport slows further oxidation.
A compact, strongly adherent oxide scale prevents premature scale failure and helps preserve alloy durability.
FeNiCuAl-based multiprincipal-element alloys have insufficient oxidation resistance at temperatures of 900 °C and above.
Engineered interfacial segregation will produce a significantly slower oxide-growth rate than a homogeneous baseline alloy.
Engineered interfacial segregation will produce a thinner oxide scale than the homogeneous baseline.
Engineered interfacial segregation will improve oxide adherence and reduce scale spallation relative to the homogeneous baseline.
The proposed segregation-controlled behavior should hold during cyclic oxidation from 800 °C to 1200 °C.
Mixed or ternary oxides and other microstructural changes may also affect oxidation behavior.
Oxidation of compositionally complex alloys can produce layered oxide films through species transport and outward cation diffusion.
Under some high-temperature oxidation conditions, mixed Mn-Cr or Mn-Fe oxides can form instead of binary Cr or Fe oxides.
A controlled comparison should use samples with identical overall composition but different levels of grain-boundary or interfacial segregation.
Oxide thickness, adhesion or spallation, elemental enrichment, and mass-change kinetics are measurable observables for testing the hypothesis.
Failure of the engineered samples to show a statistically significant improvement over the homogeneous controls would falsify the proposed governing role of segregation.
